The Hopewell people built in earth the way others build in stone. About two thousand years ago, in the valleys of southern Ohio, they raised enormous banks, circles, squares and octagons, some enclosing many hectares, and aligned them to the sun and moon. Seip Earthworks, in the valley of Paint Creek in Ross County, is part of the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, which were inscribed as a World Heritage site in 2023, and the group also includes the Octagon Earthworks at Newark and the High Bank Works near Chillicothe. They were not forts or farms, but meeting places for gatherings, feasts and funerals.

What survives at Seip is a large burial mound, one of the biggest of its type, which was excavated in the early twentieth century and found to hold many burials, copper ornaments, mica cutouts, pearl beads and pipes carved in the form of animals. The Hopewell traded across the continent, bringing obsidian from the Rockies, shells from the Gulf of Mexico and copper from the Great Lakes, and the objects found in their mounds show an elaborate culture. The earthen walls of the main enclosure, a circle, a square and an adjoining mound, were levelled by ploughs over the years, but traces remain and the National Park Service has marked out the lines.

For riders, southern Ohio is a pleasant surprise. The hills of the Appalachian foothills are steep and wooded, and the country roads wind through farmland, forest and small villages, with a lot of curves and little traffic. The Hocking Hills region, about an hour's ride to the east, is famous for its sandstone gorges and waterfalls, and for some of the best motorcycle roads in the Midwest. Highway 50, along the Paint Creek valley, is a smooth and fast road with views of the river. Autumn colours in October are spectacular, and the summers are warm and humid, with thunderstorms.

Greenfield, nineteen kilometres away, has about forty-five hundred people and the nearest fuel and meals, and Frankfort is a smaller village. Chillicothe, the first state capital, is the main city of the region, and it has the main visitor centre for the park. Watch for deer on the roads, especially at dusk.
t.hopeton earthworks@39.4,-83.0:
Ohio is not the place you expect to find ancient geometry, but the Hopewell people built it here. Hopeton Earthworks lies on a terrace above the Scioto River just north of Chillicothe, and it is one of the sites listed by UNESCO in 2023 as the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks. These mounds and enclosures were built roughly two thousand years ago, and the scale is hard to grasp from the ground because many of the walls are low and softened by farm fields and time. The shapes were circles, squares and octagons, set out with a precision that suggests careful planning.

What makes the Hopewell culture interesting is how far it reached. People here exchanged goods across much of eastern North America: obsidian from the Rockies, copper from Lake Superior, mica from the Appalachians, shells from the Gulf coast. The earthworks were not houses or forts. They were ceremonial centres, probably linked to astronomy and funerary rites, and some of them align to lunar cycles in a way that continues to attract research. Nearby Octagon Earthworks in Newark is the best-known example, while Seip and High Bank are other sites in the same family.

The riding here is gentle, rolling and green. Ohio's back roads are straight in the river bottoms and bend a little where they climb onto the ridges, and you ride past farms, corn and soybean fields and small villages with churches and diners. Surfaces are mostly decent, speeds modest, and the main risks are tractors, deer at dusk and the odd gravel patch where a field track meets the road. Late spring and early autumn are best, when the corn is high or the colours are turning.

Chillicothe, about six kilometres away, has about twenty thousand people and everything you need: fuel, food, motels and a historic downtown. It was the first capital of Ohio and the Scioto valley around it is full of old farmhouses and older stories. Take a walk on the grass at the site, read the interpretive panels, and remember that the people who built these walls moved earth in baskets.
t.mount mitchell@35.8,-82.3:
Mount Mitchell has a simple claim to fame: at 2,037 metres, or 6,684 feet, it is the highest point in the United States east of the Mississippi River. It stands in the Black Mountains of western North Carolina, part of the southern Appalachians, and a spur road climbs to the summit from the Blue Ridge Parkway at around milepost 355. The last stretch of the road ends at a car park a short walk below the summit, where an observation platform gives views across rows of blue ridges.

The mountain is named for Elisha Mitchell, a professor from the University of North Carolina who measured the peak in the 1830s and argued about its height with a rival. In 1857 he fell from a cliff near a waterfall while returning to confirm his measurements, and was buried at the summit, where his grave still lies. The area became North Carolina's first state park in 1915, after logging companies had stripped much of the forest, a loss that prompted early conservation efforts in the state.

The high slopes hold a forest more typical of Canada. Red spruce and Fraser fir grow here, cool and dark, and the air smells of resin on damp mornings. Sadly, many of the Fraser firs have been killed by an invasive insect, the balsam woolly adelgid, leaving grey skeletons among the green. Clouds often wrap the summit, and temperatures at the top can be 10 degrees Celsius lower than in the valley. Snow can fall in any month except high summer.

The Blue Ridge Parkway is a famous motorbike road, with a low speed limit, long gentle bends and constant views, and the climb up the spur to the summit is a short, steep detour. Sections of the parkway and the spur road close in winter, with ice and fog, so check the status before setting out. Autumn colours in October draw crowds. Black Mountain, seventeen kilometres away, and Burnsville have petrol stations and places to eat. Pack a warm layer, even in July.
t.high bank works@39.3,-82.9:
Most people expect an ancient monument to be made of stone. High Bank Works is made of earth, and it asks you to do a little more of the work yourself. It sits in the Scioto Valley a few miles south of Chillicothe, Ohio, on flat bottomland that looks like any other farm field until you notice the low grassy banks drawing a perfect circle joined to a perfect octagon. The Hopewell people raised these walls roughly two thousand years ago, with baskets of soil, no draft animals and no metal tools.

What makes it more than a pretty lawn is the geometry. The octagon and its neighbouring circle are laid out so exactly that researchers have argued for decades that the alignments track the lunar cycle, including the long 18.6 year swing of the moon's rising points. Nobody can tell you for certain what the ceremonies were. The Hopewell traded obsidian from Wyoming, shell from the Gulf and copper from Lake Superior across half a continent, and this was clearly a place where that world came together. Together with the Newark Great Circle in the north of the state, Mound City in Chillicothe and the other earthworks on these rides, it was added to the UNESCO list in 2023, which tells you the scholars take it seriously.

The riding around here is gentle Ohio, and honest about it. Southern Ohio is where the glaciers stopped, so the country starts to roll and fold into wooded hills a little to the east and south, and the lanes along the Scioto and Paint Creek are pleasant, lightly trafficked and best in late spring when the corn is low or in October when the sycamores along the river turn. Expect farm trucks, the odd slow tractor and gravel on the shoulders at field entrances. Nothing here will test you. The pleasure is rolling from one earthwork to the next and noticing how the land was chosen.

For practical matters, Chillicothe, about seven kilometres off, has fuel, food and beds, and it was Ohio's first state capital, so the old downtown is worth a slow lap on a bike. The site itself is open and has little shade, so in July bring water and a hat. Walk the bank rather than ride toward it, read the signs, and give yourself ten quiet minutes to imagine the crowds that once gathered here.
t.sochi@43.6,39.7:

Sochi has plenty of fuel stations and workshops. The food is varied, with grilled meat and cheese pastries in the Caucasian style, and the local wine and tea. The best months for riding are May, June and September, when the water is warm and the crowds thin. Rain can be heavy in autumn and winter.
t.shady valley@36.5,-81.9:
Shady Valley is a quiet bowl of farmland tucked among the high ridges of north-east Tennessee, close to the Virginia line, and for motorcyclists it is a pilgrimage point. Locals hold a cranberry festival each autumn, and the little community around the old general store feels far from anywhere.

The tarmac is generally good, the camber helpful and the surroundings beautiful, with rhododendron thickets and hardwood forest closing in on both sides. Treat it with respect. Gravel, wet leaves in autumn, oncoming trucks and the occasional car wandering over the centre line have caused many accidents, and police patrol the route with some enthusiasm. A relaxed pace is both safer and a lot more enjoyable.

Nearby Backbone Rock, a narrow ridge pierced by a short railway tunnel that now carries a road, is a curiosity worth seeing. Spring brings flowering dogwood and redbud, and October is brilliant with leaf colour, though that is also the busiest time. Summer afternoons can bring sudden thunderstorms.

Fuel and food are the things to plan. Shady Valley is tiny, so the dependable stations are in Mountain City, about thirteen kilometres away, and in Abingdon, Virginia, a graceful old town with a good theatre and a historic centre, about twenty kilometres further. Mountain City has diners and motels, and Abingdon has more. Fill up before you commit to the mountain, carry a rain jacket, and expect to share the road with other riders.
t.the snake us 421@36.5,-81.9:

Mountain City, eight and a half kilometres from here, is the nearest town, and Abingdon, in Virginia, about twenty-two kilometres away, is the nearest larger town with the full range of services. t.tazewell food@37.1,-81.5:
Tazewell is a small town in the mountains of south-west Virginia, the eastern doorstep to a road known as the Back of the Dragon. The surrounding hills are coal country, and in the nearby valleys the mines have shaped the local economy and culture for generations.

On the road toward Marion, the scenery is lovely. The forest is thick with oak, maple, hickory and rhododendron, and in spring the redbud and dogwood bloom along the roadside, while in autumn the ridges blaze with colour. Wildlife is plentiful, with deer and sometimes black bears, and fog can settle in the hollows. Richlands, about twenty-four kilometres away, is the nearest town with more services. Try a country breakfast, with biscuits, gravy and sausage, or a plate of barbecue and beans, which are staples of the area. t.asheville@35.6,-82.5:
Asheville lies in a bowl of the Blue Ridge, where the French Broad River slides past old brick warehouses and the mountains stand on every side in layers of blue. At about six hundred and fifty metres it is cooler than the Carolina lowlands in summer, and the air smells of woodsmoke and wet leaves in autumn. It still stands on its estate, with gardens by Frederick Law Olmsted, and it is the largest private house in the country. Downtown holds a good deal of Art Deco architecture, built in the 1920s before the Depression stopped the boom, and the whole district is walkable, with bookshops, cafes and a lively food scene. Craft breweries have made Asheville famous, with dozens in a small area.

For a motorcyclist the Blue Ridge Parkway, which runs for 469 miles along the crest of the mountains, is the great attraction. In summer, afternoon storms come quickly, and in the morning, fog fills the valleys, rising slowly as the sun burns it off. t.great smoky mountains national park@35.6:
The Smokies get their name from the haze. Water vapour and natural compounds released by the forest rise from the ridges and form a blue-grey mist that settles in the valleys, so that the mountains look like layers of smoke. They are among the oldest mountains on Earth, worn down for hundreds of millions of years, and rounded and green. This is the most visited national park in the country, and strangely, it charges no entry fee.

The pin falls on the North Carolina side, near the Oconaluftee and Deep Creek areas, not far from Cherokee. The Eastern Band of Cherokee live here, and their history in these mountains goes back thousands of years. The road to know is Newfound Gap Road, US 441, which crosses the main crest at 1,539 metres and runs between Cherokee and Gatlinburg. It climbs through a series of forest zones that resemble a drive from Georgia to Canada, from oak and hickory to spruce and fir. The curves are gentle and wide, the surface is mostly good, and the pace is slow and heavily trafficked in summer and October. A side spur leads to Clingmans Dome, at 2,025 metres the highest point in the park, with an observation tower.

Wildlife is rich. Black bears are abundant, and elk have been reintroduced at Cataloochee, with herds often seen in the fields at dusk. The park is known for its salamanders, with more species than almost anywhere else in the world, and in early summer, fireflies in one valley flash in synchrony. Fog and cloud are common, and rain can arrive suddenly at the higher elevations, with temperatures falling by ten degrees.

Cherokee and Bryson City on the south side and Gatlinburg and Pigeon Forge to the north are the nearest services. A parking tag is required if you stop for more than fifteen minutes, so buy one before you go. In winter, the road may close for snow or ice, so check ahead before committing to the climb.
t.ferapontovo@60.0,38.6:
Ferapontovo is a village of a few thousand people in the forest country of Vologda, and it holds one of the great treasures of Russian art. The Ferapontov Monastery, founded in the late fourteenth century by a monk named Ferapont, stands on a low hill between two lakes, and the white walls and golden domes of its cathedral are reflected in the water. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the reason is inside: the walls of the Nativity Cathedral are covered in frescoes painted in 1502 by Dionisius, the most celebrated icon painter of his age.

The frescoes are unlike most Russian church painting. Dionisius used light, airy colours, soft blues, pinks, and greens, and long, graceful figures that seem to float. The effect is calm, luminous and almost musical, and many visitors find it moving even without knowing the stories. Photography is restricted, and the cathedral is small, so visits are short and the light inside is dim, so give your eyes a moment. A museum on the site tells the story of the monastery, which was closed in the Soviet era and later restored.

The ride here is a gentle one through the north Russian taiga. The roads run through flat, wooded country with birch and spruce, wide skies, small villages of weathered wooden houses with carved window frames, and glimpses of lakes. Surfaces vary from decent asphalt to patched and potholed, and trucks use the main road, so take care on blind rises. The white nights of June, when the sky never gets fully dark, are magical, but mosquitoes in summer can be a nuisance, and winters are long and bitterly cold.

Kirillov, about fourteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with a proper range of services and has fuel and shops. It also holds the Kirillo-Belozersky Monastery, a huge fortified complex founded in 1397, with thick walls and towers beside a lake. Belozersk, further north, is another old town worth seeing. Local food includes rich Vologda butter and fish from the lakes. Foreign visitors should check carefully what is currently possible before planning a trip.
t.tellico plains@35.4,-84.3:

The town is small, with a main street, a few cafes and a general air of being at the end of the road, which in a sense it is. It was built over some thirty years and opened in 1996, and it was designed with gentle gradients and wide curves, so it is smooth and easy, a more relaxed counterpart to the famous tight twisting of the Tail of the Dragon, which lies farther south.

Food is easy in town, with diners serving breakfast, burgers and barbecue, and a coffee and a biscuit make a good start. In peak season, weekends bring many bikes, so earlier is better.

t.trabzon@41.0,39.7:

It dates, according to tradition, from the fourth century, and the painted walls and the sheer drop are astonishing, though the walk up can be steep and crowded. The coast road, the D010, runs east toward Rize and Georgia, with the sea on one side and mountains on the other. The real riding begins when you turn inland, where side valleys offer long climbs into the Kaçkar range and a gradual shift from coastal humidity to alpine air. Rain is frequent, mist is common, and you should pack waterproofs even in summer.

t.back of the dragon@37.1,-81.5:

t.robbinsville@35.3,-83.8:

t.tazewell@37.1,-81.5:
Tazewell is a small Appalachian county seat in southwest Virginia, and the road that matters here is Virginia Route 16, the one that riders call the Back of the Dragon. Route 16 has a poor reputation for accidents, and with good reason: the curves tighten without warning, the surface is variable and sometimes damp under tree cover, and cattle and deer can appear on the pavement. The best seasons are spring and mid-October, with mild days and colorful hills, though summer is green and warm, with afternoon storms. Winter ice can close the mountain road. Mist and fog gather in the hollows, so slow down in the lower sections.
t.fayetteville@38.1,-81.1:
Fayetteville is a small town beside a very large hole. The New River Gorge, a deep canyon cut by one of the oldest rivers in North America, is just outside town, and spanning it is the New River Gorge Bridge, a steel arch of about 876 feet above the water, completed in 1977. In 1870, Tsar Alexander II issued a decree creating an imperial estate on the shores of Lake Abrau, on the Black Sea coast near Novorossiysk, to develop viticulture on the southern slopes, and a few years later Prince Lev Golitsyn, who had made wine in Crimea, took over the project and began to produce champagne by the traditional method, with cellars dug into the hillside. The Abrau wines won prizes in Europe, and the tsar's court drank them. In the Soviet period, the estate supplied Soviet Champagne, the cheap and cheerful sparkling wine that appeared at every celebration, and today Abrau-Dyurso is a modern winery and a tourist stop, with tastings, cellar tours and restaurants.

The setting is lovely. The lake lies in a hollow of the Caucasus foothills, a few kilometres inland from the sea, about three kilometres long and a good deal deeper than it looks, ringed by forested hills and vineyards. The village runs along its north shore, with its neat old estate buildings, a promenade, and boats for hire, and the air smells of pine, juniper and warm stone. In summer, it is busy, with day trippers from Novorossiysk and Anapa, and in spring and autumn it is calmer. The sea beyond the ridge is warm in August.

The road from Novorossiysk climbs over a low ridge and drops to the lake, with gentle curves and good views, and the surface is generally decent, though it can be crowded in July and August. The main coastal highway between Novorossiysk and Anapa is a busier and more urban ride, with many roundabouts and speed cameras, and I would not recommend it for relaxed riding in summer. The inland roads through vineyards and hills are quieter and more enjoyable, especially in early morning. Weather is Mediterranean, with hot dry summers, wet autumns and the occasional fierce wind, called the bora, which blows down from the mountains at Novorossiysk and can make a bike twitchy.

Fuel is not sold in the village, to the best of my knowledge, and the nearest sizeable towns are Gayduk and Novorossiysk, so fill up there. The village has plenty of restaurants, cafés and guest houses, though tasting is obviously a matter of moderation if you are riding. Book tours in advance on summer weekends.

Take a walk around the lake in the evening. The light is soft, and the vines look golden.
t.anapa@44.9,37.3:
Anapa is Russia's family seaside, and everything about it is built around sand. The town sits on a low coast where the northern foothills of the Caucasus finally flatten out into the Taman steppe, and the beaches that run for tens of kilometres are broad, gentle and shallow, with water that warms quickly in summer, which makes the place a favourite for parents with small children. The sand is real, unlike the pebbles farther south, and the dunes along the Bugaz spit to the north form a protected landscape of grass and sand beside the Black Sea lagoons.

The history goes back to the Greeks. Under the name Gorgippia, a Greek colony and later a major city of the Bosporan Kingdom stood here, and some of its streets and houses have been excavated and preserved in an open-air museum in the middle of the modern town. Later, the Ottomans fortified Anapa in 1781 as a base on the Circassian coast, and Russian troops took it in 1790, then again in 1828, and what remains of the fortress walls can be seen near the lighthouse. The town was heavily damaged in the Second World War and rebuilt as a resort, with wide avenues, sanatoria and promenades.

For a rider, Anapa is a place of flat ground, wide roads and heavy summer traffic. The coastal highway from Novorossiysk and the roads into town can be packed in July and August, and the speed cameras are many. Spring and autumn are far better, with warm air, calm seas and open roads, and from May to June and September to October the region is at its best. Vineyards and orchards stretch inland, and the roads through them are flat and easy, with long straights and mild curves. Winds can be strong, especially in the late autumn, and rain arrives in squalls.

Everything you need is here. Petrol stations line the main roads, cafés and restaurants serve fish, grilled meat and local wine, and the hotels range from basic guest houses to large holiday complexes. In high season, accommodation is expensive and fills quickly, so book ahead. The town has a lively market, and the smell of grilled mackerel and peaches follows you down the streets.

Walk out onto the sand at sunset, and watch the sea turn pink. Families come out in droves, and the whole beach feels like a long, cheerful evening.
t.guamka@44.2,39.9:
Guamka lies at the mouth of the Guam Gorge, a narrow slot in the limestone where the Kurdzhips River comes down from the Caucasus. The gorge is about a kilometre and a half long, and in places the walls rise several hundred metres, so close together that the sky is a thin strip and the light is dim even at noon. Ferns and moss cling to the rock, and the river has cut smooth, curved shapes into the stone. It is a spectacular place, and for nearly a century, it has drawn travellers who come to see a piece of the mountains that can be reached without climbing a peak.

The reason it is so accessible is a railway. In the twentieth century, a narrow-gauge line was built through the gorge, and a tiny train with a few carriages still runs along the cliff, crossing the river on small bridges, and carrying visitors in the summer season. It is slow, rattling, and lovely, and it is a part of the area's character. A walking path follows the line, and at the upper end of the gorge there is a cluster of small cafés and stalls selling honey, herbs and tea. I would check whether the train is operating before you plan to ride it.

The surrounding country is the western Caucasus: steep forested slopes of beech, oak and fir, with limestone cliffs and caves. Bears, wild boar and deer live in the hills, though you are unlikely to see them, and in spring, the ground is covered with snowdrops and primroses. Mezmay, a village a short distance away, is a popular base for walkers.

For riders, the roads here are among the most enjoyable in the region, away from the busy Black Sea coast. The route from Apsheronsk climbs through the foothills in long, gentle curves, with the gorge opening dramatically ahead. The surface is generally decent, though patchy, and there can be gravel and mud near the gorge. Weekends in summer are crowded, so go early. Rain can arrive suddenly, and the gorge is slippery in wet weather, so wear shoes with grip if you plan to walk. September is a very good month, with fewer visitors and warm days.

Fuel is available in Apsheronsk, about twenty-nine kilometres away, and in Kamennomostsky, so fill up before you come. Neftegorsk and the smaller villages have basic shops, and the cafés at the gorge serve hot food and tea. Look up from the bottom of the gorge, and notice how small the sky becomes. It is an old, deep, quiet place.

Among the fields of the Paint Creek valley in southern Ohio, a few kilometres from Chillicothe, lies a patchwork of low grassy ridges that once formed one of the largest earthwork enclosures in North America. The Hopewell Mound Group is the site that gave its name to the whole Hopewell culture, which flourished in the Ohio valley from about 200 BC to AD 500. It was named after Mordecai Cloud Hopewell, on whose farm it stood in the nineteenth century. The enclosure originally surrounded about a hundred hectares, with walls and many mounds, and archaeologists have found rich deposits of ceremonial objects within.

The Hopewell people did not live here in a city; they gathered for ceremonies and burials, and their exchange network spanned the continent. Copper came from the Great Lakes, mica from the southern Appalachians, obsidian from the Yellowstone region, and shells from the Gulf of Mexico, all turned into ornaments, headdresses and effigies of birds and animals. The sheer scale of the earthworks, laid out with astronomical alignments, speaks of a society that organised labour and ritual on a grand scale. UNESCO listed the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks in 2023, together with the nearby Octagon and High Bank Works.

What remains today is subtle. The walls are gentle rises in the grass, the old mound outlines are marked by mown patches, and a walk across the site on a cold morning, with mist on the field and the oaks bare, gives a calm, thoughtful feeling. It rewards people who like to imagine the past more than those who want grand monuments.

The ride is a pleasure in itself. The roads around Chillicothe cross rolling farmland and wooded hills at the edge of the Appalachian plateau, with long curves, little traffic and fine views. East of town lies the Hocking Hills region, with sandstone gorges, hemlock woods and waterfalls, and the roads there are some of the best in the state. Autumn colours in October are spectacular, summer is warm and humid, and winter can bring ice.

Chillicothe, with about twenty-two thousand people, was the first capital of Ohio, and it has fuel, cafes and good places to stay. Smaller places near the site, like North Fork Village and Frankfort, offer less, so plan fuel in town. A diner breakfast of eggs, biscuits and gravy is the traditional start of a day in these parts.

Its 153 precast segments, each slightly different, were lifted into place one by one. When it opened, the whole Parkway, begun in the 1930s, was finally complete, in 1987, after more than fifty years.

The result is a road that looks like a ribbon draped over the rock. The viaduct curves in a continuous S-shape, and riding across it, with the mountain on one side and a drop through the trees on the other, feels like flying. Below, the forest is a mixture of hemlock, rhododendron and hardwoods, which in autumn is a blaze of colour. The visitor centre at the viaduct has an exhibit explaining the construction, and a short trail runs under the bridge so you can see the piers up close.

Grandfather Mountain itself, a few kilometres away, is one of the oldest mountains on earth, and one of the most biologically diverse in the Appalachians, with rare plants and animals. t.craggy gardens@35.7,-82.4:

t.waterrock knob@35.5,-83.1:

t.deals gap@35.5,-83.9:

t.puerto lopez@-1.6,-80.8:

t.dillard@35.0,-83.4:

t.lake bogoria@0.3,36.1:
Lake Bogoria lies at the bottom of the Rift Valley in central Kenya, a long, narrow, alkaline lake squeezed between a steep fault wall on the west and a flat, thorny plain on the east. t.sibiloi national park@4.0,36.3:
Sibiloi sits on the eastern shore of Lake Turkana, which is one of the most remote places in Kenya, and getting there is an expedition rather than a day ride. The park was created to protect fossils. t.central island@3.5,36.1:

t.south island@2.6,36.6:
South Island is the southern of Lake Turkana's three island parks, a low, bare, volcanic outcrop in the south of the lake, near the settlement of Loiyangalani. t.lake turkana national parks@3.1,36.5:

Upstream dams on the Omo have raised concerns about how the water level will behave in the future, a worry that fishing families here follow closely.

The listing recognises the fossil beds, the breeding of Nile crocodiles, the wintering birds and the geology of the rift. The approach from the south runs through Isiolo, Marsabit and across the lava fields, some paved, much of it gravel, sometimes with sand and washouts. Distances between towns are great. During the middle of the day the heat is close to unbearable, and the lake looks flat and white. Plan your riding for the early hours, rest in the shade, and carry plenty of water. The dry months from June to October are best.
t.cherokee@35.5,-83.3:

t.pudozh@61.8,36.5:
Pudozh is a wooden-roofed river town on the Onega, about a hundred kilometres east of the great lake of the same name, in the far north of Karelia where the land is flat, forested and soaked with water. It is a place of about ten thousand people and a long history, first mentioned in the fifteenth century, when it was a trading post on routes between the White Sea and Novgorod. The river is broad and slow, and the whole area is a mosaic of swamps, birch woods and lakes.

t.belozersk@60.0,37.8:
Belozersk sits on the southern shore of Lake Beloye, the White Lake, and it is one of those Russian towns whose age is difficult to grasp. The chronicles say that Sineus, a brother of the legendary Viking chief Rurik, ruled here in the ninth century, and while historians treat the story with care, the town has certainly been important since the Middle Ages. They enclose a quiet area of wooden houses, churches and a museum, with the lake spreading out beyond. Even more special is the small Ferapontov Monastery, whose cathedral is covered inside with frescoes painted around 1502 by the master Dionisy, in glowing, delicate colours of blue, pink and white. Belozersk has fuel, shops and a few cafés, and the local speciality is fish from the lake, especially smelt, which are caught in great numbers and fried or served in a clear fish soup called ukha. Summer is short and green, with long evenings, while autumn colours arrive in September, and winter freezes the lake solid.
t.tuapse@44.1,39.1:
Tuapse is a port town squeezed between the foothills of the Caucasus and the Black Sea, and its character is shaped by both. The mountains come down steeply here, so the town has been built in a narrow strip along the coast and up the valleys of the little rivers, with houses stacked on the slopes. About sixty thousand people live here. The name comes from the Adyghe language and is often translated as two waters, a reference to the two rivers that flow into the bay, and the area was Circassian land until the mid nineteenth century, when the Russian army conquered the coast and the Circassians were forced to leave.

Ships anchor in the bay, and the smell of salt and fuel mixes with the sea breeze. A few kilometres away, the shoreline becomes more attractive, with pebble beaches and rocky headlands. The Kiselyov Rock, a huge sea stack that rises from the water near the beach, is the town's emblem, and an offshore group of rocks is known as the Two Brothers.

It twists along the shore, climbing over headlands and dropping into resort villages, with forest-covered mountains on one side and the sea on the other. Surface quality is generally good, but the road is busy in summer with holiday traffic, and queues can be long. Sections have blind bends and trucks crossing the centre line, so overtaking should be avoided.

The climate is subtropical, with mild winters and hot, humid summers. Palm trees and mimosa grow in the town, and the mountains behind catch the clouds, so heavy rain and sudden storms occur. In autumn, the sea is still warm and the crowds thin out, which is the best time to ride. Landslides after storms occasionally block the road.

Tuapse has fuel stations on the main road, supermarkets and many small cafés. The local specialities are fresh fish, grilled or fried, and the seasonal fruit sold at roadside stalls, including grapes, persimmons and plums. Top up your tank here before the coastal sections, which have long stretches without services.
t.novorossiysk@44.7,37.8:
Novorossiysk occupies a deep bay on the northeastern shore of the Black Sea, and the first thing locals mention about it is the wind. The bora, a cold, dry gale that pours down from the mountains in winter, can blow at more than forty metres a second, strong enough to knock down fences, freeze spray on ships and force the port to close. It happens a few times a year, and the Novorossiysk bora is known across the Black Sea region. The town sits at the edge of the Caucasus, where the mountains drop to the sea, with a low pass behind it.

The city's history is a story of ports and war. It was founded in 1838 as a Russian fort, grew into a major port for exporting grain and later oil, and became a naval base. In the Second World War it was the scene of fierce fighting, and a small bridgehead on the western side of the bay, known as Malaya Zemlya, was held by Soviet troops for more than a year against German attack. A large memorial complex now stands there, and the city holds the title of Hero City. Cement is also a major industry, and the quarries and factories give parts of the town a white dusty look.

The Russian tsar Alexander II set up a royal winery here in 1870, with French techniques, and the cellars still produce Russian champagne. The coastal roads around Novorossiysk are varied. To the north, the road to Anapa runs along cliffs and steppe, with views of the sea, and the surface is generally decent. To the southeast, the road toward Gelendzhik climbs over a forested ridge and offers sea views. Summer traffic is heavy, and in winter strong winds can make riding on exposed sections uncomfortable.

Fuel and services are easy in the city, which has a population of a quarter of a million. The sea is warm from July to September, the best months for the coast are May and September, and the bora season is from November to March, so check the forecast.
t.manta@-1.0,-80.7:

t.mound city@39.4,-83.0:

t.fort ancient@39.4,-84.1:

t.velikaya guba@62.1,35.2:
Velikaya Guba is a village on the Zaonezhye peninsula, a long finger of land that stretches into Lake Onega and holds some of the most distinctive landscapes in Karelia. The name means Big Bay, and the place sits on a sheltered stretch of the shore, with the lake spreading wide and grey to the horizon and low islands scattered across it. The old Karelian and Russian traditions of the North, with their songs, laments and epics, were recorded here in the nineteenth century, and the area has been a source for collectors of folklore and for painters. Wooden houses with carved window frames and big stoves, small chapels, and fish drying on racks are still part of the scene.

For riders, the roads on the peninsula are narrow and winding, with sharp bends and frost heaves, and some sections are unpaved. They are slow and beautiful, with sudden views of the lake between the trees. Distances are modest but the going is slow, so allow plenty of time. The best season is summer, from June to August, when the days are long and the water is calm, and the worst is the spring thaw, when mud and flooding affect the roads.

There is little in the way of services, and fuel must be arranged beforehand in Petrozavodsk or Medvezhyegorsk. A few small shops sell basic supplies, and homestays offer meals of fish and potatoes. It is a place to slow down and listen.
t.kizhi ferry approach@62.1,35.2:
The island of Kizhi lies a short boat ride off the Zaonezhye coast, and the approach to the ferry is the doorway to one of the most remarkable collections of wooden architecture in the world. The pogost, a church enclosure on the island, has been a UNESCO site since 1990. Its centerpiece is the Transfiguration Church, built in 1714, with twenty-two onion domes rising in tiers like a pile of silver scales. Local legend says it was built with only an axe and without a single nail, and the carpenter threw his axe into the lake when he finished, declaring that there would never be another like it.

Beside it stands the Church of the Intercession, built in 1764, with nine domes and a warmer, more domestic character, used in the winter when the larger church was too cold to heat. A tall bell tower, built in the nineteenth century, completes the ensemble. Around them, the island is now an open-air museum, with farmhouses, barns, windmills and chapels moved here from villages across Karelia, and the grass is cut in the traditional way. The Transfiguration Church has been under restoration for years, and it is often partly covered in scaffolding, so check the current state if the view of the domes is the goal.

The place feels magical on a calm morning, when the lake lies flat and the domes reflect in the water. Weather can change fast, and the crossing can be rough when the wind is up. Visits are possible mainly in summer, when hydrofoils and ferries run from Petrozavodsk and from villages on the peninsula, and in winter the island is reached across ice. Tickets and timetables are best checked in advance.

For riders, the approach by road is part of the experience. The road along the peninsula is narrow and winding, with forest on both sides and occasional views of the lake, and it requires a relaxed pace. Expect some gravel and frost damage, and plan for mosquitoes in the warm months. Motorcycles must be left on the shore.

Services are limited, so fill the tank in Petrozavodsk or in a larger town before the approach. A simple cafe at the landing serves tea and snacks, and in season, local families sell berries and smoked fish.
t.kargopol@61.5,38.9:
Kargopol is one of the oldest towns in the Russian North, set on the Onega River in a landscape of lakes, bogs and forest that has changed little for centuries. Chronicles mention it in the twelfth century, and it grew into an important trading place on the routes to the White Sea. Today it is a quiet town of about eleven thousand people with a surprising number of old churches, many of them in white stone with green or silver domes, and the streets are lined with low wooden houses with carved window frames.

The town is known for its folk crafts. The Kargopol clay toy, with its bright geometric patterns in red, white and green on a pale clay body, is a symbol of the region. The most famous figure is Polkan, a mythical creature that is half man and half dog. The craft was kept alive by a few families in the twentieth century and is now sold across Russia. The local museum has a fine collection of icons, textiles and wooden objects, and the Cathedral of the Nativity, built in the sixteenth century, is a landmark.

The countryside around Kargopol is part of the Lake Lacha basin and leads to the Kenozero National Park, a region of lakes and old villages that holds some of the best-preserved wooden chapels and houses in Russia. The roads are a mix of paved and gravel, with sections that become soft after rain. Distances are long and traffic is light, which suits slow travel. The best time to go is summer, from June to August, though in July the mosquitoes can be ferocious. Autumn brings a golden light and fewer insects. Winter is long and cold, with roads under snow.

Practical matters need planning. Kargopol has fuel stations, basic hotels and a few cafes, but the villages beyond are small and have few services, so fill up and carry food and water. Phone coverage can be thin in the forest. The town is far from large centers, and repair shops are limited.

Walk along the river in the early evening and watch the swallows over the water. The sound of church bells carries a long way over the flat land.
t.lazarevskoye@43.9,39.3:
Lazarevskoye is the southern end of Greater Sochi, a long ribbon of beach towns that runs along the Black Sea coast beneath the western foothills of the Caucasus. The village was founded in the nineteenth century as a fort and named after Admiral Mikhail Lazarev, a navigator and naval commander who took part in the early exploration of Antarctica. Today it is a resort district of about thirty thousand permanent residents, though the population swells in summer, when holidaymakers fill the guesthouses, sanatoriums and cafes that line the shore.

The setting is subtropical, and that is surprising for Russia. Palms, magnolias, bamboo and tea bushes grow on the slopes, and the mountains behind rise steeply, covered in beech and oak forest, to peaks that carry snow into early summer. The beaches are mostly pebbles and the sea is warm from July to September, but it can be rough in storms, and heavy rain in autumn and winter sometimes floods the small rivers that rush down from the hills. The Caucasus Biosphere Reserve lies inland, protecting some of the wildest mountain forest in Europe, including bison, bears and lynx.

For riders, the coastal highway is the main route, running along the foot of the mountains between Tuapse and Sochi. The surface is good, but traffic is the issue. In summer, the road is crowded with cars, buses and trucks, and traffic jams can last for hours, particularly on weekends and in the evening. Motorcycles can slip through, but the heat and fumes make it tiring. The best seasons are May, June and September, when the sea is warm and the crowds thinner. Early morning is calmer in any month.

The roads leading inland up the river valleys offer a quieter alternative. They climb through forest and past waterfalls, with tight bends and steep gradients, and they give a sense of the mountains that stand behind the coast. Surfaces vary, and some sections are narrow and steep, so check locally.

Services are everywhere, with fuel stations, supermarkets, restaurants and repair shops in the resort zone. Prices are higher in summer, and accommodation fills quickly in July and August, so book ahead. Try grilled fish, shashlik and local tea. Walk onto the pier in the evening and watch the light fade over the water. The mountains turn blue, and the sea is calm.
t.dzhubga@44.3,38.7:
Dzhubga is where the Black Sea highway stops pretending to be a quiet coast road and shows you what it really is: a single ribbon squeezed between steep, forested Caucasus foothills and a pebble shoreline, shared with every truck and holiday car on this side of Russia. The village sits at the mouth of a small river, about halfway between Gelendzhik to the northwest and Tuapse to the southeast, with Lermontovo a few kilometres down the shore and Novomikhaylovskiy a little further on.

For a rider it is a working stop rather than a scenic one. With a little over five thousand people it has the petrol stations and cafes you want, and further south the supply thins out between the resort villages, so top the tank here if you are heading toward Tuapse. The surrounding riding is better than the town itself. North and south of Dzhubga the road rises and drops across headlands, with long gentle bends, short tunnels of trees and sudden glimpses of grey-green sea. Traffic is the real variable. In July and August the coast road crawls, and you will spend more time filtering through queues of cars with roof boxes than leaning into corners. Go in May, June or September, or leave at first light, and the same asphalt feels like a different road entirely.

Dzhubga has a harbour with an oil terminal, which explains the tankers that sit on the horizon, and that industrial edge gives the place a more honest feel than the polished resorts nearby. The beach is pebbles rather than sand, and the water is clear on calm days. Behind the village the hills are covered in oak, hornbeam and beech, thinning to scrub where the slopes face the sun, and in the evening you can smell warm resin and sea salt together, which is a combination I have never found anywhere else.

The coast is also a place of old layers. Circassian peoples lived along these valleys before the nineteenth-century Caucasian war pushed them out, and Russian settlement followed with the military line and later the resort boom. Little of that is visible at the roadside, but the river valleys that cut inland are worth a glance on the map, because side roads into them quickly turn quiet and green.

Treat Dzhubga as a good place to refuel, eat something grilled and let your shoulders drop before the next run of headlands. Keep an eye on the weather as well, because summer storms roll in off the sea quickly and the road gets slick.
t.gelendzhik@44.6,38.1:
Gelendzhik wraps itself around one of the best natural bays on the Russian Black Sea, a nearly closed bowl with a long spit across its mouth, and it has used that gift to become one of the country's biggest summer resorts. The city has just over fifty thousand permanent residents and many times that number in July, which tells you most of what you need to know about parking and traffic. Divnomorskoye lies a few kilometres to the southeast and Kabardinka a little further the other way toward Novorossiysk.

Riding in is easy and pleasant, riding around is slow. The highway from Novorossiysk crosses low, dry hills with views opening over the bay, and from the south you come over wooded headlands before the city appears below you. Inside town you are on a seafront promenade, plane trees, ice-cream queues and roads that were never meant to carry this many cars. If you want the corners, they are outside: the coast roads and the climbs into the hills behind, where the surface is generally decent and the bends tighten gently. Early morning is the right hour, before the beach crowds wake up.

Gelendzhik was a fortress before it was a resort. The Russian military founded it in the 1830s as part of the line along this coast, during the long Caucasian war, and for decades it was a small garrison town. The change came in the Soviet period, when sanatoria and holiday houses multiplied along the shore, and the fashion has never really left. The seafront today is polished and busy, but it is still a place where families on a fortnight's holiday stroll slowly past grilled fish and fruit stalls.

The landscape behind the city is worth knowing. The hills here are dry compared with the lush coast further south, covered in juniper and oak scrub, and the air carries a distinct herbal smell on hot days. The coast is also a famous region for wine, and the grapes you pass on the slopes are the reason the coastal hills around Abrau-Dyurso, a short ride west, have such a name for sparkling wine.

For practical purposes, Gelendzhik has everything: fuel, food at every price, accommodation, and mechanics if something goes wrong. It is the sensible place to eat properly and plan the next day. Just do not expect solitude between June and September.
t.apsheronsk@44.5,39.7:
Apsheronsk is a railway-and-oil town of about forty thousand people tucked into the forested foothills of the Western Caucasus, on the Pshekha River, with Khadyzhensk a short ride to the northwest and Neftegorsk, an oil settlement, to the south. It is the staging post for the ride into the Guamka Gorge, a famous narrow canyon cut into the rock, and it works as the practical lungs of the route: fuel, food, a bed and a mechanic if you need one.

Do not expect charm from the town itself. It is a Soviet-era working place of apartment blocks, markets and filling stations, with a station on the Armavir-Tuapse line that has hauled goods and passengers to the coast for a century. The name comes from the Apsheron Regiment, a Russian military unit from the Caucasian war, and the town grew where the army and then the railway wanted it. The oil is real too: the Apsheronsk and Neftegorsk fields are among the oldest in Russia, and you will see pumpjacks nodding in the fields and forest clearings, which is an odd and rather beautiful sight with mountains behind.

Out of town, the riding gets better quickly. The road south follows the river through mixed forest of oak, hornbeam and beech, with the valley closing in and the surface variable but mostly decent. Corners are medium radius and flowing rather than tight, and you can keep a steady rhythm. Traffic is light outside holiday weekends, though trucks use some stretches. The Guamka Gorge itself is a short distance from the main road, and the locals know it for its narrow limestone walls, and the rock paths that lead in from the road. Spring and early summer bring the best green, autumn the best colour, and winter can bring ice in the shaded sections.

Nature around here is rich. The forests host deer and wild boar, bears keep to the higher slopes, and in summer the hills hum with insects and birdsong. The river runs clear and cold over stones, good for a quick splash of water on the face on a hot day.

Fill up here before heading in. Past the last villages the roads thin out, and phone coverage drops in the narrow gorge. Pack a warm layer, because the mountain air cools quickly in the evening, and allow time for the ride out.
t.tapoco cheoah dam@35.5,-83.9:
Cheoah Dam is a curved wall of concrete at the bottom of one of the most famous motorcycle roads in the world, and it is also, rather improbably, a film location. In the 1996 movie The Fugitive, Harrison Ford's character leaps from the top of a dam into the water below, and that dam is this one, high above the Cheoah River in the mountains of western North Carolina, close to the Tennessee line. You can see it from the road, and a surprising number of riders stop just to stand where the film crew stood.

The dam was built in 1919, in a hurry and in the middle of nowhere, for the Aluminum Company of America, which needed cheap hydroelectric power to smelt aluminium for the First World War effort and beyond. The company built a whole company community called Tapoco, a name made from the initials of the Tallassee Power Company, and a lodge is still there. The setting is lovely: wooded ridges, the green Little Tennessee River backed up behind the dam, and steep, narrow valleys covered in oak, hickory and rhododendron.

Just a few miles from here is the road that has made this area famous: US 129, the Tail of the Dragon, which famously packs around three hundred curves into eleven miles between this part of North Carolina and Tennessee. It is a tight, technical, fast road with no side roads and no houses, and it is popular with riders and sports cars alike. Cheoah Dam is a good place to catch your breath before or after it. The nearby Cherohala Skyway, a long, smooth mountain road that climbs from Robbinsville toward Tellico Plains, is a gentler, higher cousin, with views over the Unicoi range.

Services around the dam are limited. Fuel is sold at Robbinsville, about eighteen kilometres away, and at the motorcycle resort in Deals Gap near the start of the Dragon, and food, souvenirs and photographs of your bike on the Dragon are all easy to find there. Riding here demands attention: gravel in the corners, cars drifting over the line and police patrols are all common, and speeding fines are heavy. Be kind to your tyres, keep to your side of the line, and enjoy the quieter pleasure of a hot afternoon beside the water.
t.cherohala skyway point 1@35.4,-84.3:
The town sits on the Tellico River at the foot of the mountains in Monroe County, Tennessee, a quiet place of a few hundred people with a general store atmosphere, a small main street and one or two stations. The sensible habit is to fill the tank here, buy something to eat, and only then turn onto Tennessee 165, the road that becomes the Cherohala Skyway as it climbs.

The skyway itself is a curious piece of American public works. Planned in the early 1960s to link Tellico Plains with Robbinsville, North Carolina, across the Unicoi Mountains, it took decades to finish because the ridge is steep and the engineers had to blast and bridge their way over and around it. It opened in 1996. The name stitches together Cherokee and Nantahala, the two national forests it crosses, and the project cost a fortune for a road with no real commercial reason to exist. That is exactly what makes it a joy: it was built for the view and the drive.

The Tellico valley below is Cherokee country. Tellico was an important Cherokee town before European settlers arrived, and the nearby Overhill towns were the centre of the Cherokee world in the eighteenth century. The Tellico River itself is a famous trout stream, cold and clear and tumbling over boulders, and the forest above it is dense hardwood, which turns spectacular in October.

For the rider, the first miles out of town are a gentle warm-up. The road follows the river through shaded woods, with easy bends and a good surface, and the rhythm gradually tightens as the grade increases. It is a road for smooth riding rather than heroics, with long, well-engineered curves and few blind corners, but the traffic can include logging trucks, drivers who stop suddenly for photographs and wandering deer at dusk.

Tellico Plains is small, so Athens, about twenty-eight kilometres to the west, is the nearest sizeable town if you need anything more. The skyway is usually open year-round, but high sections can ice over in winter, so check conditions if you are riding between November and March. Spring comes late to the top, where redbud and dogwood are still in flower weeks after the valley has gone to leaf.
t.cherohala skyway point 2@35.3,-84.0:
Up here the skyway earns its name. You are on the high spine of the Unicoi Mountains, somewhere near the line where Tennessee gives way to North Carolina, with the road running along the ridge at well over five thousand feet. The air is noticeably cooler than in the valleys on either side, and on a summer day you might swap a sticky ninety degrees at Tellico Plains for a damp sixty here. In winter the same ridge can be sheathed in rime ice while the valleys are dry.

The vegetation changes with the altitude. Lower down, it is oak and hickory. Up here, the forest thins into northern hardwoods and, in places, spruce and fir, with grassy openings called balds. The reason for those balds remains something of a mystery, though grazing, fire and weather have all been proposed. Overlooks along this section give views across successive blue ridges, the layered look that gave the Smokies their name.

The riding is superb for anyone who likes steady, rhythmic curves. The road is wide, well surfaced and engineered, with banking that rewards a smooth line, and the speed limit is modest, which you may find helpful because the hazards are not the bends but the other users: cyclists grinding up the climbs, motorists parked at overlooks and the occasional bear crossing. Gravel sometimes washes onto the road after heavy rain, so look ahead at the exits of corners.

There are no services on this section at all. Robbinsville is the closest town and it is more than twenty kilometres away, and Andrews and Murphy are further. Make sure your tank is full before you set off from either end, and carry water and a warm layer. Mobile phone coverage is patchy to absent on the ridge.

The best time to ride it is a weekday in late spring, when the rhododendron and mountain laurel are in flower and the traffic is light, or a clear autumn morning when the leaves are at their peak. Summer weekends bring a lot of motorcyclists and sports cars, and the upper stretches can be shrouded in fog. If the cloud closes in, slow down and wait for it to lift, because the views are the point.
t.foothills parkway point 4@35.8,-83.2:
Most people never see this end of the Foothills Parkway, which is exactly why you should. It lies on the north-eastern edge of the Great Smoky Mountains near Cosby, a sleepy community that has a reputation as an old moonshine country and still feels somewhat apart from the tourist bustle on the Tennessee side. The short eastern section of the parkway runs along the ridge above the valley, with long views across farmland to the high peaks.

The Cosby area is the quiet door into the national park. A road leads up to a campground and trailheads among tall hemlocks and rhododendrons, and the Cosby section of the park is known for its wildflowers, which burst in April and May. It sees a fraction of the visitors who crowd the Gatlinburg entrance, and many people consider that a blessing. The surrounding hills were home to mountain families for generations, and the old log cabins and stone chimneys still show up in the forest if you walk far enough.

For the rider, the eastern parkway is a gem of calm. It is short, smooth and almost empty, with long gentle curves along the ridge and a speed limit that suits a relaxed pace. You can pull over at overlooks and have the view to yourself. The road itself is a good example of the parkway's character: wide, well engineered, with a gradual rhythm that settles you into the saddle.

Newport, about eighteen kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size and has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Cosby itself has a couple of small stores. Plan to fill up in Newport or on the main road, since the parkway has no services. US 321 and the back roads around Cosby give a gentle loop through farm country, with tobacco barns and old churches along the way.

The best time of year is spring, when wildflowers carpet the forest floor, or autumn, when the ridge turns red and gold. Summer is hot and humid, with frequent afternoon thunderstorms. Early mornings are cool, mist hangs in the hollows and the valley feels timeless. If you like quiet roads and the sense of finding a place that others miss, this is it.
t.blue ridge parkway point 3@36.7,-80.4:
Mabry Mill has to be the most photographed building on the parkway, and for once the cliche is justified. A little red-brown mill, with a big overshot water wheel turning beside a pond and a wooden flume carrying water to it, stands among rhododendrons beside the road. It was built by Edwin Boone Mabry in the early 1900s, and for decades it ground corn and sawed timber for neighbours who farmed these hills. Today it is a living museum, with demonstrations of blacksmithing, weaving and milling in the summer months.

The little restaurant beside the mill is a long-standing parkway tradition, famous for its buckwheat pancakes and cornmeal, and it is a good place to refuel. Be ready for queues at weekends in the high season. The parkway here runs through country of old hill farms, split-rail fences and meadow, and the ridge is a rolling upland more than a sharp crest.

This corner of Virginia is the heartland of old-time mountain music. The Crooked Road, a heritage trail of venues, passes through, and in the nearby town of Floyd, a little to the north-east, the country store hosts a Friday night jamboree where fiddlers, banjo players and flatfoot dancers fill the floor. Visitors are welcome, and it has become a pilgrimage for fans of bluegrass and traditional music. Even if you do not stay for the music, a drive into the town is a nice detour.

The riding on this stretch is easy and relaxed. Long, gentle curves run through meadow and woodland, with wide views of rolling farmland, and the road surface is consistently good. At this latitude and altitude, the spring comes late and the rhododendrons bloom in June, making a pink and white fringe along the roadside. In autumn, the surrounding hills glow with colour and the apple stands at the roadside open for business.

Stuart and Floyd are the nearest towns, each with a petrol station and basic shops, while Mount Airy, about thirty kilometres away, is bigger. Weather is changeable and can turn foggy and cool, so carry a layer. If the mill is busy, wait for a quiet moment, and you will see the wheel and pond at their best in the soft light of early morning.
t.blue ridge parkway point 6@35.8,-82.3:
Mount Mitchell is the highest point in the eastern United States, at 6,684 feet, and a short spur road from the parkway leads almost to the top. The mountain is named for Elisha Mitchell, a professor at the University of North Carolina who measured the peak in the 1830s and died in a fall near the summit in 1857, while trying to prove his claim against a rival. He is buried at the top, under a stone tower, and the peak has been a state park since 1915, the oldest in North Carolina.

Arriving at the summit is a strange experience. The temperature is often twenty degrees cooler than in the valley, the air smells of spruce and fir, and the trees are stunted and twisted by the wind. These high forests are a remnant of the ice age, with plants and animals that belong more to Canada than to the Carolinas, and they are under threat. An insect from Europe, the balsam woolly adelgid, has killed many of the Fraser firs, and acid rain has added to the damage, leaving grey skeletons among the green.

For the rider, the road to the summit is Route 128, a short, steep, twisting climb off the parkway, with a modest speed limit and a few tight corners. The surface is generally good, but it can be wet or icy, and fog is common. There is a small restaurant at the top in summer, and a short paved trail leads to the observation platform, from which you can see layer after layer of blue ridges. The visitor centre has displays on the mountain's history and geology.

Black Mountain, about seventeen kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town, with fuel and food, and Burnsville, a little further, is smaller. Plan to fill up before you go up the spur, and bring a warm layer and a waterproof, even in July. The summit often sits in cloud, and the views come and go with the weather, so a clear day is a gift.

The best time to visit is early on a weekday in autumn, when the lower slopes blaze and the crowds are thin. In winter the road closes when snow and ice build up, and in spring it opens when conditions allow. Check the park's website before you go, because the weather here can change the plan.
